job.style: a conversation between a teacher and two students

response.passage: Teacher: Today, let us explore the globe. Rohan, do you think the lines on the map are real painted lines on the ground? Rohan: Yes, I thought they were painted lines. Teacher: Actually, latitudes and longitudes are imaginary circles drawn by geographers to help us locate places. Priya: Does that mean the Torrid Zone is hot because it is physically closer to the sun? Teacher: Not at all, Priya. The Torrid Zone receives maximum heat because the sun's rays fall vertically on this region, not because of distance. Rohan: If I travel east, will the time be the same as my home? Teacher: No, time changes with longitude. Since the Earth rotates from west to east, places east of Greenwich see the sun earlier. Priya: Is the Indian Standard Time based on the Prime Meridian? Teacher: No, India uses 82.5° E longitude as its standard meridian because it passes through the center of our country. Finally, remember that unlike latitudes, which are parallel circles, all longitudes converge at the poles. This is why they are not parallel to each other. If you look at a globe, you will see that longitudes meet at the North and South Poles, unlike the latitude lines that run horizontally around the sphere.
response.summary: The passage explains that latitudes and longitudes are imaginary lines used for navigation and timekeeping. It clarifies that heat zones depend on the angle of sun rays, and time varies based on longitude rather than a universal standard.
